verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘The set feasts of Yahweh, which you shall proclaim to be holy convocations, even these are my set feasts.
“‘Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, a holy convocation; you shall do no kind of work. It is a Sabbath to Yahweh in all your dwellings.
“‘These are the set feasts of Yahweh, even holy convocations, which you shall proclaim in their appointed season.
In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening, is Yahweh’s Passover.
On the fifteenth day of the same month is the feast of unleavened bread to Yahweh. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread.
In the first day you shall have a holy convocation. You shall do no regular work.
But you shall offer an offering made by fire to Yahweh seven days. In the seventh day is a holy convocation: you shall do no regular work.’”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,

“Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘When you have come into the land which I give to you, and shall reap its harvest, then you shall bring the sheaf of the first fruits of your harvest to the priest:
and he shall wave the sheaf before Yahweh, to be accepted for you. On the next day after the Sabbath the priest shall wave it.
On the day when you wave the sheaf, you shall offer a male lamb without defect a year old for a burnt offering to Yahweh.

The meal offering with it shall be two tenths of an ephah  of fine flour mingled with oil, an offering made by fire to Yahweh for a pleasant aroma; and the drink offering with it shall be of wine, the fourth part of a hin.

You must not eat bread, or roasted grain, or fresh grain, until this same day, until you have brought the offering of your God. This is a statute forever throughout your generations in all your dwellings.
“‘You shall count from the next day after the Sabbath, from the day that you brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven Sabbaths shall be completed:
even to the next day after the seventh Sabbath you shall count fifty days; and you shall offer a new meal offering to Yahweh.
You shall bring out of your habitations two loaves of bread for a wave offering made of two tenths of an ephah  of fine flour. They shall be baked with yeast, for first fruits to Yahweh.

You shall present with the bread seven lambs without defect a year old, one young bull, and two rams. They shall be a burnt offering to Yahweh, with their meal offering, and their drink offerings, even an offering made by fire, of a sweet aroma to Yahweh.
You shall offer one male goat for a sin offering, and two male lambs a year old for a sacrifice of peace offerings.
The priest shall wave them with the bread of the first fruits for a wave offering before Yahweh, with the two lambs. They shall be holy to Yahweh for the priest.
You shall make proclamation on the same day: there shall be a holy convocation to you; you shall do no regular work. This is a statute forever in all your dwellings throughout your generations.

“‘When you reap the harvest of your land, you must not wholly reap into the corners of your field, and you must not gather the gleanings of your harvest. You must leave them for the poor, and for the foreigner. I am Yahweh your God.’”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, shall be a solemn rest to you, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, a holy convocation.
You shall do no regular work; and you shall offer an offering made by fire to Yahweh.’”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,

“However on the tenth day of this seventh month is the day of atonement: it shall be a holy convocation to you, and you shall afflict yourselves; and you shall offer an offering made by fire to Yahweh.
You shall do no kind of work in that same day; for it is a day of atonement, to make atonement for you before Yahweh your God.
For whoever it is who shall not deny himself in that same day; shall be cut off from his people.
Whoever it is who does any kind of work in that same day, that person I will destroy from among his people.
You shall do no kind of work: it is a statute forever throughout your generations in all your dwellings.
It shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for you, and you shall deny yourselves. In the ninth day of the month at evening, from evening to evening, you shall keep your Sabbath.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to the children of Israel, and say, ‘On the fifteenth day of this seventh month is the feast of tents for seven days to Yahweh.
On the first day shall be a holy convocation: you shall do no regular work.

Seven days you shall offer an offering made by fire to Yahweh. On the eighth day shall be a holy convocation to you; and you shall offer an offering made by fire to Yahweh. It is a solemn assembly; you shall do no regular work.

“‘These are the appointed feasts of Yahweh, which you shall proclaim to be holy convocations, to offer an offering made by fire to Yahweh, a burnt offering, and a meal offering, a sacrifice, and drink offerings, each on its own day;
besides the Sabbaths of Yahweh, and besides your gifts, and besides all your vows, and besides all your freewill offerings, which you give to Yahweh.

“‘So on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you have gathered in the fruits of the land, you shall keep the feast of Yahweh seven days: on the first day shall be a solemn rest, and on the eighth day shall be a solemn rest.
You shall take on the first day the fruit of goodly trees, branches of palm trees, and boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook; and you shall rejoice before Yahweh your God seven days.
You shall keep it a feast to Yahweh seven days in the year. It is a statute forever throughout your generations. You shall keep it in the seventh month.
You shall dwell in temporary shelters  seven days. All who are native-born in Israel shall dwell in temporary shelters,
that your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in temporary shelters,  when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.’”
Moses declared to the children of Israel the appointed feasts of Yahweh.

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks to Moses about time itself—not random days, but marked days. When God names what matters, He gives His people a rhythm to follow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These are 'set feasts'—boundaries God draws around holy time. Notice how the Lord calls them 'my feasts,' not the people's. Even our worship belongs to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Sabbath sits here at the heart—every seventh day, work stops, and rest becomes holy. In a world that never sleeps, God still teaches: you are more than what you produce.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each feast comes in its 'appointed season.' God doesn't rush His people; He writes their worship into the very fabric of the year, making grace rhythmic and sure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Passover, on the fourteenth evening—every year, the people remember being passed over, spared from death. That mercy is never old; it's retold in every generation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven days of unleavened bread follow the Passover lamb. Haste and hurry belong to the old Egypt; here, the people learn to eat bread without the leaven of their old ways.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The first day is 'holy convocation'—the work stops, the people gather. There's wisdom in stopping together, remembering together, who you are together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even in the feast week, three days are marked for holy rest—the first and seventh especially. God's people learn that freedom doesn't mean endless motion; it means His rhythm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again, the Lord speaks to Moses. Each feast receives its own careful word. When God details what He treasures, He shows us what to treasure too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sheaf of first fruits—the harvest begins, but not for the people first. The priest brings the first bite to the Lord. Giving God the first teaches the giver: all is His gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest waves the sheaf 'to be accepted for you.' Someone stands between, lifting what grows from the earth, asking the Lord to see it through their hands. Intercession is ancient.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A young lamb, whole and without defect—the first fruits need first sacrifice. The Lord doesn't ask for scraps; He asks for what costs, which shows He's worth it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Flour mingled with oil, wine poured out—each offering has its precise form, its meal and its drink. Worship isn't sloppy; detail itself becomes love's language.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No one eats the new grain until the offering is made—hunger must wait. This statute teaches the young what the old know: there is an order to blessing, and patience honors it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fifty days counted from sheaf to Pentecost—a week of weeks. This is math made holy, turning calendar pages into spiritual arithmetic.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After those fifty days, another offering appears: a new meal offering. The cycle turns; the Lord keeps drawing His people to times of remembrance and gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two loaves baked with yeast—unusual in offerings. This bread rises; it's living, active. Pentecost celebrates the Lord at work in the people, the harvest made grain made bread.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven lambs, one bull, two rams—the number seven marks it as God's feast, the offerings speak of power and sacrifice. The Lord welcomes His people with abundance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A sin offering and peace offerings sit side by side—acknowledging failure and sealing reconciliation. Before the feast meal, the people are made clean.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest waves the offerings—they become the priest's portion. Those who serve the altar eat from it. The Lord feeds His servants from His own table.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Proclamation, rest, no work—the feast day itself declares the Lord's character. Stopping work becomes testimony; rest becomes praise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even in the feast, the poor are remembered—leave the corners, gather no gleanings. The Lord's generosity to His people overflows to those who have little. Grace multiplies when shared.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks again to Moses, turning now to the seventh month. After spring feasts comes autumn's remembrance—He doesn't let His people forget the whole year belongs to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The feast of trumpet blasts—a 'memorial of blowing.' Sound carries across a distance; it gathers scattered people, calls them home. The Lord's voice still summons.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No work, but an offering by fire—even the day of trumpet calls is marked by gift. The Lord doesn't ask His people to simply stop; He bids them to give.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again, the Lord speaks. The feasts build in rhythm, each word from His mouth deepening how the people understand His character—careful, intentional, close.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Day of Atonement, the tenth of the seventh month—'you shall afflict yourselves.' This is the feast where sorrow and healing meet, where a people faces what separates them from God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No work at all—the whole day stands still before God. On this day, the people learn that standing before the Lord means stopping everything else; that is the whole of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To refuse to afflict oneself, to refuse the fast—this cuts one off from the people. Rejecting the day of reconciliation means rejecting the community it heals. We belong or we don't.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The warning is severe: anyone who works on this day 'shall be destroyed from among his people.' The Lord takes this day seriously—not as rule, but as the hinge where His people turn back to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This statute, forever and everywhere—Atonement Day doesn't fade with time or distance. In every generation, in every dwelling, the people return to the place where they are reconciled.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Evening to evening—the Sabbath of Atonement crosses a whole day and night. From dusk to dusk, the people rest in the shadow of forgiveness. Even time itself bends toward healing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks to Moses once more. The feasts arrive in layers—first reconciliation, then joy. The Lord's way is to bring His people home before He bids them celebrate.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Feast of Tents, seven days in the seventh month—a dwelling made of branches, a remembrance made concrete. The people live as their ancestors lived, not in stone but in memory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The first day is holy convocation, no work—the feast begins in rest. Before the celebration begins, the people stop and gather, centering on the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven days of offerings, an eighth day of solemn assembly—the feast doesn't end in exhaustion but in another holy convocation. Joy itself closes in reverence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These appointed feasts gather the whole offering: burnt, meal, sacrifice, drink—each one a language the people speak to say 'You are God.' The vocabulary of worship is rich.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beside the Sabbaths, the gifts, the vows, the freewill offerings—the feasts don't replace devotion; they frame it, contain it, make room for it. Worship builds on worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Feast of Tents comes 'when you have gathered in the fruits'—not before, not in hope, but after harvest, in gratitude. The Lord's feasts teach: first the work, then the thanks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Palm fronds, thick boughs, willows—the people decorate their tents with branches, turning dwellings into gardens. Even temporary shelter becomes a place of beauty when made for joy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Feast of Tents is kept in the seventh month, forever—each year, the people remember they were tent-dwellers, strangers, pilgrims. This feast says: you belong to the Lord, not to any place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven days dwelling in temporary shelters—for one week, the people trade their houses for branches. They learn again: homes are real, but they are not forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The reason: 'I made the children of Israel to dwell in tents when I brought them out of Egypt.' This feast is not ritual; it is memory, annually renewed. The Lord is the God who brought you out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses declares all these feasts to Israel—he speaks the Lord's word into the people's calendar. When God's word is spoken aloud by His servant, the year itself becomes instruction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
